This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,

L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference

sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.

oral-bioavailability outcome.

records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Small polar polyhydroxy compounds with physicochemical profiles comparable to ascorbic acid show oral bioavailability at or above the 20% threshold: mannitol 63% in healthy adults and ~20-24% in patients, sorbitol 36-38%, glucose 38-84%, and propylene glycol very high.

Additional polar or small-molecule contexts also support F >=20%: topiramate >80%, frusemide ~40%, gallium maltolate 25-57%, pipemidic acid 93%, and diflunisal 89.5%, although structural transferability is lower for some of these.

The only coherent low-F context, gemcitabine (10%, poor/low), is attributed to first-pass metabolism by cytidine deaminase and is not transferable to ascorbic acid, which lacks that metabolic liability.

The physicochemical prior's unfavorable passive permeability is an uncertain prior, and its own caveat notes that active transport (SVCT1/2) could significantly enhance ascorbic acid absorption; the empirical pattern of high F in polar small molecules supports F >=20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for ascorbic acid is present in the supplied cards; all support is transfer-based.
Mannitol data at high colonoscopy doses are borderline (~20-24%) and may be dose- or patient-dependent.
Active transport (SVCT1/2) and dose-dependent absorption of ascorbic acid are not directly measured in the cited records.
The frusemide context card's canonical SMILES does not match the named drug, reducing confidence in that card's transferability.

The physicochemical prior is uncertain and does not outweigh this empirical pattern.
